questions.q: Which of the following is a proposition?
choices: Austin is the capital of Texas.
questions.explain: A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both. 'Austin is the capital of Texas' is a declarative sentence with truth value T. A question and a command have no truth value. The tempting choice is 'x + 1 = 2': it looks like a statement, but its truth depends on the unassigned variable x, so it is not a proposition until x is given a value.

questions.q: Let p be true, q be false, and r be true. Which compound proposition is TRUE?
questions.explain: p ⊕ r is T ⊕ T = F, and ¬q = T, so (p ⊕ r) ∨ ¬q = F ∨ T = T. Check the others: p ∧ q = T ∧ F = F; (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬r = T ∧ F = F; p ⊕ r = F because exclusive or is false when both parts are true. The tempting trap is treating ⊕ like ∨ and calling p ⊕ r true.

questions.q: Let p = 'Sam takes calculus' and q = 'Sam takes physics.' Translate: 'Sam takes calculus or physics, but not both.'
questions.explain: 'One or the other but not both' is exclusive or, p ⊕ q, which is equivalent to (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q). p ∨ q is inclusive (it is also true when Sam takes both), which is the most common mistake. (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∧ q) forgets the negation and just says 'both'.

questions.q: Let p = 'The concert is sold out' and q = 'Tickets were cheap.' Translate: 'The concert is sold out, but tickets were cheap.'
questions.explain: In logic, 'but' means 'and' (it only adds a sense of contrast in English). Both facts are asserted, so the translation is p ∧ q. The tempting wrong answer is p ∧ ¬q, which reads the contrast word 'but' as a negation. Nothing in the sentence says tickets were not cheap.

questions.q: In this course, when is the disjunction p ∨ q true?
choices: Only when both p and q are true
When at least one of p, q is true
When exactly one of p, q is true
questions.explain: ∨ is always inclusive: p ∨ q is T when p is true, q is true, or both are true. It is F only when both are false. 'Exactly one' describes exclusive or (p ⊕ q), the usual mix-up.

questions.q: Which is the truth-table column for p ⊕ q, with rows in the order (p, q) = TT, TF, FT, FF?
questions.explain: p ⊕ q is true exactly when p and q have different truth values: TT→F, TF→T, FT→T, FF→F. T,T,T,F is the column for inclusive p ∨ q (the common mix-up). T,F,F,F is p ∧ q, and T,F,F,T is p ↔ q, which is the negation of ⊕.

questions.q: What is the negation of 'x is greater than 5' (x > 5)?
questions.explain: ¬(x > 5) must be true for every x that does NOT satisfy x > 5. That includes x = 5 and everything below it, so it is x ≤ 5. 'x < 5' is the classic mistake: it leaves out x = 5, so x = 5 would make both the statement and the 'negation' false. (Compare Assignment 1: ¬(x ≥ 3) is x < 3.)

questions.q: What is the negation of 'The store is not open on Sunday'?
choices: The store is open every day.
The store is closed on Sunday.
The store is not open on Monday.
The store is open on Sunday.
questions.explain: Negating ¬p gives ¬¬p ≡ p, so the negation is simply 'The store is open on Sunday.' 'The store is closed on Sunday' is tempting, but it means the same thing as the original sentence. 'Open every day' asserts much more than the negation does.

questions.q: Using the standard precedence (¬ first, then ∧, then ∨, then →, then ↔), how is ¬p ∨ q ∧ r grouped?
questions.explain: ¬ applies only to the symbol right next to it (p). Next, ∧ binds tighter than ∨, so q ∧ r is grouped first. The result is (¬p) ∨ (q ∧ r). The tempting ((¬p) ∨ q) ∧ r just reads left to right and ignores that ∧ has higher precedence than ∨. In practice, use parentheses even when the precedence is known.

questions.q: Which is the truth-table column for ¬p ∧ (p ∨ q), rows (p, q) = TT, TF, FT, FF?
questions.explain: Work from the innermost operations outward. ¬p = F,F,T,T and p ∨ q = T,T,T,F. Their conjunction is F∧T, F∧T, T∧T, T∧F = F, F, T, F. F,F,T,T is just the ¬p column, which is what you get if you forget to AND it with p ∨ q in the last row.

questions.q: How many rows does the truth table of a compound proposition with 4 distinct propositional variables have?
questions.explain: Each variable is T or F, so n variables give 2ⁿ combinations: 2⁴ = 16. 8 = 2³ is the count for three variables (an off-by-one in the exponent). 4 rows is the count for two variables.

questions.q: Which of the following is a compound (not atomic) proposition?
choices: It is cold and it is windy.
questions.explain: An atomic proposition cannot be broken into simpler propositions. A compound proposition combines propositions with logical operators. 'It is cold and it is windy' is p ∧ q. The other three are single atomic statements. '7 is a prime number' might look complex, but it contains no connective.

questions.q: Which truth assignment makes ¬p ∧ (q ∨ r) true?
choices: p = T, q = T, r = T
p = T, q = F, r = T
p = F, q = F, r = F
p = F, q = F, r = T
questions.explain: We need ¬p true (so p = F) and at least one of q, r true. p = F, q = F, r = T gives T ∧ (F ∨ T) = T. Both assignments with p = T fail because ¬p is F. p = F, q = F, r = F fails because q ∨ r is F.

questions.q: For which truth values is the conditional p → q FALSE?
questions.explain: p → q only makes a claim about what happens when p occurs. It is broken only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false (T → F). If p is false the conditional is vacuously true, which is why the p-false rows are tempting but wrong.

questions.q: What is the truth value of: 'If Houston is the capital of Texas, then sloths are reptiles'?
choices: False, because the conclusion is false
False, because both parts are false
True, because the hypothesis is false
questions.explain: Let p = 'Houston is the capital of Texas' (F) and q = 'Sloths are reptiles' (F). A conditional is false only in the case T → F. F → F is vacuously true, so the statement is True. It is tempting to call it false because both parts are false, but p → q makes no claim at all when p is false.

questions.q: What is the contrapositive of 'If it rains, then I bring an umbrella'?
choices: If I do not bring an umbrella, then it does not rain.
It rains and I do not bring an umbrella.
If I bring an umbrella, then it rains.
If it does not rain, then I do not bring an umbrella.
questions.explain: The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p: negate both parts AND swap them. 'If I bring an umbrella, then it rains' is the converse (q → p), and 'If it does not rain…' is the inverse (¬p → ¬q). Those two are the usual mix-ups. 'It rains and I do not bring an umbrella' is the negation p ∧ ¬q.

questions.q: What is the converse of 'If n is divisible by 6, then n is even'?
choices: If n is not even, then n is not divisible by 6.
n is divisible by 6 and n is not even.
If n is not divisible by 6, then n is not even.
If n is even, then n is divisible by 6.
questions.explain: The converse of p → q is q → p: swap hypothesis and conclusion without negating. 'If n is not even, then n is not divisible by 6' is the contrapositive, the most common confusion. 'If n is not divisible by 6, then n is not even' is the inverse. Note the converse here is false (n = 2) even though the original is true.

questions.q: Which statement is logically equivalent to p → q?
questions.explain: A conditional is always equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p. The converse q → p and the inverse ¬p → ¬q are not equivalent to p → q (check the row p = T, q = F). ¬q ∨ p is equivalent to q → p, the converse, not to p → q (which is ¬p ∨ q).

questions.q: Which pair of statements built from p → q are logically equivalent to EACH OTHER?
choices: The conditional p → q and its converse q → p
The converse q → p and the inverse ¬p → ¬q
The contrapositive ¬q → ¬p and the converse q → p
The conditional p → q and its inverse ¬p → ¬q
questions.explain: The inverse ¬p → ¬q is the contrapositive of the converse q → p, so those two are equivalent. The conditional is equivalent only to its contrapositive, not to its converse or inverse. Assuming a statement implies its own converse is one of the most common logic errors.

questions.q: Let p = 'I pass the class' and q = 'I study.' Translate: 'I pass the class only if I study.'
questions.explain: 'p only if q' means p cannot happen without q: if p happens, q must have happened, so p → q. The trap is q → p, because 'if' appears right before q. But 'only if' introduces the conclusion, not the hypothesis.

questions.q: 'Having a ticket is necessary for boarding the plane.' Which conditional expresses this?
choices: If you board the plane, then you have a ticket.
If you have a ticket, then you board the plane.
You board the plane if and only if you have a ticket.
If you do not board the plane, then you do not have a ticket.
questions.explain: 'q is necessary for p' means p → q, with q = 'you have a ticket' and p = 'you board.' Anyone who boards must have a ticket. The reversed version says that having a ticket guarantees boarding, which is the sufficiency reading and not what was stated.

questions.q: 'A sufficient condition for the warranty to be good is that you bought the computer less than a year ago.' Which conditional expresses this?
choices: If you did not buy the computer less than a year ago, then the warranty is not good.
If the warranty is good, then you bought the computer less than a year ago.
The warranty is good only if you bought the computer less than a year ago.
If you bought the computer less than a year ago, then the warranty is good.
questions.explain: 'p is sufficient for q' means p → q: the sufficient condition (recent purchase) is the hypothesis. The second and third choices both say 'warranty good → bought recently,' which treats the purchase as necessary. The last choice is the inverse.

questions.q: Let r = 'It rains' and b = 'I go to the beach.' Translate: 'I go to the beach unless it rains.'
questions.explain: 'q unless p' means 'if not p, then q.' So 'b unless r' is ¬r → b (equivalently r ∨ b). The tempting b → ¬r claims that going to the beach guarantees no rain, which is a different statement. ¬r ∧ b asserts both facts outright instead of a conditional.

questions.q: Which is the truth-table column for p ↔ q, rows (p, q) = TT, TF, FT, FF?
questions.explain: p ↔ q is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value: TT→T, TF→F, FT→F, FF→T. T,F,T,T is the column for p → q, which is easy to confuse with ↔. F,T,T,F is p ⊕ q, and T,T,F,T is q → p.

questions.q: Which biconditional is TRUE?
choices: 5 is odd if and only if 7 is even.
1 + 1 = 3 if and only if the moon is made of cheese.
Austin is the capital of Texas if and only if 1 + 1 = 3.
2 + 2 = 4 if and only if 3 is even.
questions.explain: p ↔ q is true when both sides have the same truth value. In the first choice both sides are false (F ↔ F), so it is true. Each other choice pairs a true statement with a false one (T ↔ F), so each is false. Many people assume a biconditional of two false statements must be false.

questions.q: What is the contrapositive of 'If x > 2, then x² > 4'?
questions.explain: Contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p. ¬(x² > 4) is x² ≤ 4 and ¬(x > 2) is x ≤ 2. 'If x² > 4, then x > 2' is the converse, and 'If x ≤ 2, then x² ≤ 4' is the inverse. 'If x² < 4, then x < 2' negates > as < and so drops the equality cases.

questions.q: Suppose p → q is FALSE. What is the truth value of its converse q → p?
choices: Cannot be determined from the given information
It has the same value as p → q, whatever that is
questions.explain: p → q is false only when p = T and q = F. Then q → p is F → T, which is True. You might expect the converse to share the conditional's truth value, but it does not: here they differ, which also shows the two are not equivalent.

questions.q: What is the output of this circuit?
questions.code:
Gate 1: NOT(q)
Gate 2: AND(p, Gate 1)
Gate 3: OR(Gate 2, r)
Output = Gate 3
questions.explain: Trace the circuit from the inputs forward. The inverter produces ¬q. The AND gate combines p with ¬q to give p ∧ ¬q. The OR gate combines that with r: (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r. The tempting p ∧ (¬q ∨ r) puts the gates in the wrong order: the AND happens before the OR, so the AND result is inside the parentheses.

questions.q: When drawing the circuit for ¬p ∨ (q ∧ ¬r), which gate produces the final output?
choices: Either AND or OR; the order of gates does not matter
questions.explain: Work outside-in: the main (outermost) connective of ¬p ∨ (q ∧ ¬r) is ∨, so the last gate is an OR gate. Its two inputs are ¬p (from an inverter) and q ∧ ¬r (from an AND gate). The AND gate is tempting because it appears inside, but it only feeds the OR gate.

questions.q: Using one gate per logical operator, how many gates does the circuit for (p ∨ ¬r) ∧ (¬p ∨ q) need?
questions.explain: Count the operators: two NOTs (¬r, ¬p), two ORs (p ∨ ¬r, ¬p ∨ q), and one AND to combine them: 5 gates. A common miscount is 3, which forgets the inverters, or 4, which counts only one NOT.

questions.q: For which input does this circuit output 1?
questions.code:
Gate 1: OR(p, q)
Gate 2: NOT(r)
Gate 3: AND(Gate 1, Gate 2)
Output = Gate 3
questions.explain: The output is (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬r. We need r = 0 and at least one of p, q equal to 1. p = 0, q = 1, r = 0 gives (0 ∨ 1) ∧ 1 = 1. The input with all ones fails because ¬r = 0, and both p = q = 0 inputs fail because p ∨ q = 0.

questions.q: What is the output of this circuit?
questions.code:
Gate 1: NOT(p)
Gate 2: OR(q, Gate 1)
Gate 3: AND(p, Gate 2)
Gate 4: NOT(Gate 3)
Output = Gate 4
questions.explain: Build it from the inputs: Gate 1 = ¬p. Gate 2 = q ∨ ¬p. Gate 3 = p ∧ (q ∨ ¬p). Gate 4 negates the whole thing: ¬(p ∧ (q ∨ ¬p)). The tempting ¬p ∧ (q ∨ ¬p) applies the final NOT only to p instead of the whole AND output.

questions.q: Which basic gate is also called an inverter?
questions.explain: The NOT gate takes one input bit p and outputs ¬p, inverting it, so it is called an inverter. AND and OR gates take two inputs. XOR is not one of the three basic gates used in this section.

questions.q: This circuit's output is equivalent to which single connective?
questions.code:
Gate 1: AND(p, q)
Gate 2: NOT(p)
Gate 3: NOT(q)
Gate 4: AND(Gate 2, Gate 3)
Gate 5: OR(Gate 1, Gate 4)
Output = Gate 5
questions.explain: The output is (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q), which is true exactly when p and q are both true or both false. That is the definition of p ↔ q. It is easy to mistake this for p ⊕ q, but ⊕ is true when the inputs DIFFER, which is the negation of this circuit.

questions.q: This circuit's output is equivalent to which single connective?
questions.code:
Gate 1: OR(p, q)
Gate 2: AND(p, q)
Gate 3: NOT(Gate 2)
Gate 4: AND(Gate 1, Gate 3)
Output = Gate 4
questions.explain: The output is (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q): at least one input is 1 but not both, so it is exclusive or, p ⊕ q. (Assignment 1 used this form for 'exactly one of'.) p ∨ q is tempting, but it would also output 1 when both inputs are 1.

questions.q: A circuit outputs ¬(p ∨ q). Which circuit built only from NOT and AND gates gives the same output?
questions.explain: By De Morgan's law, ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q, so you invert each input and feed both into an AND gate. NOT(AND(p, q)) is ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q, which is the other De Morgan law and the usual mix-up. NOT(AND(NOT p, NOT q)) equals p ∨ q, the opposite of what we want.

questions.q: What is the output column of OR(NOT p, q) for inputs (p, q) = 11, 10, 01, 00?
questions.explain: The output is ¬p ∨ q. For 11: 0 ∨ 1 = 1. For 10: 0 ∨ 0 = 0. For 01: 1 ∨ 1 = 1. For 00: 1 ∨ 0 = 1. The column is 1,0,1,1, which is the same as p → q. 1,1,0,1 is p ∨ ¬q, what you get if you invert q instead of p.

questions.q: How many of the 8 possible inputs (p, q, r) make AND(OR(p, q), r) output 1?
questions.explain: The output is (p ∨ q) ∧ r. We need r = 1 (4 inputs), minus the one where p = q = 0. That leaves 3: (1,1,1), (1,0,1), (0,1,1). Answering 4 means counting every input with r = 1 and forgetting that p ∨ q must also be 1.

questions.q: Which gate description gives a circuit for (p ∧ q) ∨ ¬r?
choices: AND gate on p and q, fed into a NOT gate; then OR with r.
NOT gate on r, ANDed with q; then OR with p.
OR gate on q and NOT r; its output is ANDed with p.
AND gate on p and q; NOT gate on r; both outputs feed an OR gate.
questions.explain: The outermost connective is ∨, so an OR gate is last. Its inputs are p ∧ q (AND gate) and ¬r (inverter). The second choice builds p ∧ (q ∨ ¬r), the third builds ¬(p ∧ q) ∨ r (the NOT is on the wrong part), and the fourth builds p ∨ (q ∧ ¬r).

questions.q: An input p passes through three NOT gates connected in series. What is the output?
questions.explain: Each inverter flips the bit: p → ¬p → ¬¬p ≡ p → ¬p. An odd number of NOTs gives ¬p. Answering p means treating three inverters like two, i.e. assuming double negation cancels all of them.

questions.q: Which of the following is a tautology?
questions.explain: (p ∧ q) → p can only fail if p ∧ q is T while p is F, and that is impossible, so it is always true. p ∧ ¬p is a contradiction. p → q is a contingency (false at p = T, q = F). (p ∨ q) → p is false at p = F, q = T, so it is also a contingency even though it resembles the correct answer.

questions.q: Classify (p → q) ∧ (p ∧ ¬q).
questions.explain: p ∧ ¬q is exactly the case where p → q is false (¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q). So the formula is r ∧ ¬r for r = p → q and is false in every row (Assignment 1, #5). It is not a contingency: no row makes it true.

questions.q: Which of the following is a contingency?
questions.explain: A contingency is neither always true nor always false. (p ∨ q) → p is T when p = T and F when p = F, q = T. p → (p ∨ q) is a tautology (this is the addition rule). (p ∧ ¬p) → q is a tautology because its hypothesis is never true. ¬(p → p) is a contradiction.

questions.q: Which proposition is logically equivalent to ¬(p ∨ ¬q)?
questions.explain: De Morgan: ¬(p ∨ ¬q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬¬q ≡ ¬p ∧ q (double negation). Keeping ∨ (¬p ∨ q) is the typical error: De Morgan's law flips ∨ to ∧. ¬p ∧ ¬q forgets that ¬¬q = q.

questions.q: Which proposition is logically equivalent to ¬(p → q)?
questions.explain: ¬(p → q) ≡ ¬(¬p ∨ q) by the conditional-disjunction equivalence. De Morgan turns that into ¬¬p ∧ ¬q, and double negation gives p ∧ ¬q. Intuitively, the conditional is false exactly when p happens and q does not. ¬p → ¬q is tempting because it 'negates both parts,' but that is the inverse, not the negation.

questions.q: Which law justifies step 3 of this derivation?
questions.code:
¬(¬p ∧ q) ∧ (p ∨ q)
1. ≡ (¬¬p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (p ∨ q)    De Morgan
2. ≡ (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (p ∨ q)      Double negation
3. ≡ p ∨ (¬q ∧ q)            ???
4. ≡ p ∨ F                   Negation law
5. ≡ p                       Identity law
questions.explain: Step 3 rewrites (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (p ∨ q) as p ∨ (¬q ∧ q). That is the distributive law p ∨ (a ∧ b) ≡ (p ∨ a) ∧ (p ∨ b), read right to left. Absorption is tempting because p shows up in both parts, but absorption is p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p, which has a different shape.

questions.q: Which step of this derivation contains an error?
questions.code:
¬(p ∧ (q ∨ r))
1. ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬(q ∨ r)      De Morgan
2. ≡ ¬p ∨ (¬q ∨ ¬r)    De Morgan
3. ≡ (¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ ¬r    Associative
choices: Step 1: the negation should apply only to p
Step 1: De Morgan should give ¬p ∧ ¬(q ∨ r)
Step 3: the associative law does not apply to ∨
questions.explain: De Morgan always flips the connective: ¬(q ∨ r) ≡ ¬q ∧ ¬r, but step 2 keeps ∨. Step 1 is correct (¬(p ∧ X) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬X), and step 3's use of associativity is valid for ∨. The choice claiming step 1 should give ¬p ∧ ¬(q ∨ r) forgets that De Morgan turns ¬(p ∧ X) into an OR.

questions.q: Simplify p ∧ (p ∨ q).
questions.explain: This is the absorption law: p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p. If p is T, then p ∨ q is T and the whole thing is T. If p is F, the conjunction is F. Distributing to (p ∧ p) ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p ∨ (p ∧ q) gives p again. p ∧ q is a tempting but wrong 'cancellation.'

questions.q: Which proposition is logically equivalent to ¬p → q?
questions.explain: Use a → b ≡ ¬a ∨ b with a = ¬p: ¬p → q ≡ ¬¬p ∨ q ≡ p ∨ q. ¬p ∨ q is the result of forgetting to negate the hypothesis ¬p when converting. That expression is equivalent to p → q.

questions.q: Which proposition is logically equivalent to p ↔ q?
questions.explain: p ↔ q is true exactly when both are true or both are false: (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q). (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q) is p ⊕ q, the opposite. (p → q) ∨ (q → p) uses ∨ where the biconditional needs ∧, and it turns out to be a tautology. (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q) simplifies to p.

questions.q: Which proposition is NOT logically equivalent to p ⊕ q?
questions.explain: ¬p ↔ ¬q is true when ¬p and ¬q match, which is exactly when p and q match. So it is equivalent to p ↔ q, the opposite of p ⊕ q. The other three are all true exactly when p and q differ. p ↔ ¬q is the tricky one: it says p has the opposite value of q, which is exactly ⊕.

questions.q: Which proposition is NOT satisfiable?
questions.explain: ¬p ∧ ¬q forces p = q = F, and then p ∨ q is F, so (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬p ∧ ¬q is a contradiction with no solution. ¬p ∧ ¬q alone is satisfiable with p = F, q = F (Assignment 2). (p → q) ∧ p is satisfied by p = q = T, and the last choice is satisfied by p = T, q = F.

questions.q: Which truth assignment is a solution of (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ r) ∧ ¬r?
choices: p = F, q = T, r = F
p = F, q = F, r = F
p = F, q = F, r = T
p = T, q = F, r = F
questions.explain: Clause ¬r forces r = F. Then ¬p ∨ r needs ¬p, so p = F. Then p ∨ ¬q needs ¬q, so q = F. The assignment p = T, q = F, r = F is tempting because it satisfies the first clause, but it fails ¬p ∨ r.

questions.q: Two compound propositions p and q are logically equivalent (p ≡ q) exactly when:
choices: p and q are both tautologies
questions.explain: p ≡ q means they have identical truth tables, which is the same as saying p ↔ q is true in every row. If only p → q is a tautology, p implies q but they need not be equivalent (e.g. p ∧ q and p). A satisfiable p ↔ q only means the two sides agree in at least one row.

questions.q: Simplify (q ∧ ¬q) ∨ (p ∧ T).
questions.explain: By the negation law, q ∧ ¬q ≡ F, and by the identity law, p ∧ T ≡ p. Then F ∨ p ≡ p, again by the identity law. Answering T confuses the identity law (p ∧ T ≡ p) with the domination law (p ∨ T ≡ T).

questions.q: In 3-SAT, what is a clause?
choices: A disjunction of literals (variables or their negations)
Any compound proposition containing exactly 3 variables
questions.explain: A clause is an OR of literals, such as (p ∨ ¬q ∨ r). 3-SAT asks whether a conjunction (AND) of such clauses, each with 3 literals, is satisfiable. That problem is NP-complete. The tempting mix-up is swapping the roles: clauses use ∨ and are joined by ∧.

questions.q: Let P(x) = 'x ≥ 3' with domain the integers. Which of the following is a proposition?
questions.explain: A propositional function is not a proposition until its variable is given a value or bound by a quantifier. P(5) = '5 ≥ 3' is a proposition (true). P(x), 'x ≥ 3', and P(x) ∧ x > 0 all still contain the free variable x, so none of them has a truth value.

questions.q: Domain: all real numbers. What is the truth value of ∀x (x² ≥ x)?
choices: True; squaring never makes a number smaller
True; it holds for x = 0 and x = 1
questions.explain: For x = 1/2, x² = 1/4 < 1/2, so the universal statement fails. One counterexample is enough to make it false. x = −1 is not a counterexample because (−1)² = 1 ≥ −1. Checking a few examples like 0 and 1 never proves a ∀ statement.

questions.q: What is the negation of 'Every student in the class has a laptop'?
choices: No student in the class has a laptop.
Some student in the class does not have a laptop.
Some student in the class has a laptop.
Every student in the class does not have a laptop.
questions.explain: ¬∀x L(x) ≡ ∃x ¬L(x): at least one student lacks a laptop. 'No student has a laptop' (∀x ¬L(x)) is the classic over-negation. It is much stronger than needed, and it says the same thing as the last choice.

questions.q: Push the negation inward so that only predicates are negated: ¬∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) ≡ ?
questions.explain: First apply quantifier De Morgan: ¬∃x(…) ≡ ∀x ¬(…). Then apply propositional De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Result: ∀x(¬P(x) ∨ ¬Q(x)). ∀x(¬P(x) ∧ ¬Q(x)) is tempting because it flips the quantifier but forgets to flip ∧ to ∨.

questions.q: Domain: all people. S(x) = 'x is a student', C(x) = 'x has taken calculus.' Translate: 'Every student has taken calculus.'
questions.explain: To restrict a ∀ to students, use a conditional: for everyone, if they are a student then they have taken calculus. ∀x(S(x) ∧ C(x)) says every person is a student and has taken calculus, the same mistake as 'every animal is a lion and fierce' in lecture. ∀x(C(x) → S(x)) reverses the direction.

questions.q: Same predicates (domain: all people). Translate: 'Some student has taken calculus.'
questions.explain: With ∃, restrict the domain using ∧: there is someone who is a student AND has taken calculus. ∃x(S(x) → C(x)) is the common error. It is true as soon as any non-student exists, because a false hypothesis makes the conditional true.

questions.q: Which is the negation of ∀x (S(x) → C(x)) ('Every student has taken calculus')?
questions.explain: ¬∀x(S → C) ≡ ∃x ¬(S → C) ≡ ∃x(S(x) ∧ ¬C(x)): some student has not taken calculus. ∃x(S(x) → ¬C(x)) is tempting, but negating a conditional does not give another conditional. ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q.

questions.q: Let the domain of x be {1, 2, 3}. Which expression is equivalent to ¬∀x P(x)?
questions.explain: Over a finite domain, ∀x P(x) ≡ P(1) ∧ P(2) ∧ P(3). Negating with De Morgan gives ¬P(1) ∨ ¬P(2) ∨ ¬P(3), which is ∃x ¬P(x). The ∧ version (equivalent to the third choice) is ∀x ¬P(x), which says every value fails rather than at least one.

questions.q: Domain: all real numbers. Which statement is TRUE?
questions.explain: ∃! means 'there is exactly one.' x² = 0 has the single solution x = 0, so the statement is true. x² = 4 has two solutions (±2), x² < 0 has none, and x > 0 has infinitely many. ∃!x(x² = 4) is the usual trap because a solution exists, just not a unique one.

questions.q: Domain: all integers. Which statement is TRUE?
questions.explain: x = 0 (or x = 1) satisfies x² = x, so the ∃ statement is true. ∀x(x² > 0) fails at x = 0. No integer squares to 2. ∀x(2x > x) fails for x ≤ 0 (for example, x = 0 gives 0 > 0, which is false).

questions.q: Domain: all integers. Which value of x is a counterexample to ∀x (x² > x)?
questions.explain: A counterexample is a domain element that makes P(x) false. For x = 1: 1 > 1 is false. For x = 2, −1, and −3 the inequality holds (4 > 2, 1 > −1, 9 > −3). Negative numbers are tempting picks, but their squares are positive and therefore larger.

questions.q: L(x) = 'x is a lion', F(x) = 'x is fierce', domain all animals. What does ∀x (L(x) ∧ F(x)) say?
choices: Every fierce animal is a lion.
Every animal is a lion and is fierce.
questions.explain: ∀x(L(x) ∧ F(x)) claims every animal in the domain is both a lion and fierce, which is clearly false. 'All lions are fierce' is ∀x(L(x) → F(x)), which uses a conditional to restrict to lions. This lecture example shows why ∀ pairs with →, not ∧.

questions.q: Q(x) = 'x has a cat', domain: students in the class. Translate: 'No student in the class has a cat.'
questions.explain: 'No student has a cat' is ¬∃x Q(x), which by De Morgan for quantifiers is ∀x ¬Q(x). ∃x ¬Q(x) and ¬∀x Q(x) are equivalent to each other and only say 'not everyone has a cat.' ¬∃x ¬Q(x) means everyone has a cat.

questions.q: L(x) = 'x is a lion', F(x) = 'x is fierce' (domain: animals). What is the negation of ∃x (L(x) ∧ ¬F(x)) ('Some lion is not fierce')?
questions.explain: ¬∃x(L ∧ ¬F) ≡ ∀x ¬(L ∧ ¬F) ≡ ∀x(¬L(x) ∨ F(x)) ≡ ∀x(L(x) → F(x)): all lions are fierce. ∀x(L(x) ∧ F(x)) is tempting, but it claims every animal is a fierce lion. ∃x(L(x) ∧ F(x)) forgets to flip the quantifier.

questions.q: L(x, y) = 'x loves y', domain: all people. Translate: 'Someone loves everyone.'
questions.explain: There is one person x such that, for every y, x loves y: ∃x∀y L(x,y). ∃y∀x L(x,y) says there is someone whom everyone loves (Assignment 2), which swaps the roles of lover and loved. ∀x∃y L(x,y) is 'everybody loves somebody.'

questions.q: Domain for x and y: all real numbers. Which nested-quantifier statement is TRUE?
questions.explain: For each x, choose y = −x, so ∀x∃y(x + y = 0) is true. ∃y∀x would need a single y that works for every x, which is impossible. ∀x∃y(xy = 1) fails at x = 0, the Assignment 2 example. Order matters when the quantifiers are different.

questions.q: P(x, y) = 'x + y = x − y', domain for x and y: all real numbers. What is the truth value of ∃y ∀x P(x, y)?
choices: False; ∃y∀x statements are never true over the reals
questions.explain: We need one y that works for every x. With y = 0, x + 0 = x − 0 holds for all x, so the statement is true. Picking x = y = 1 only shows that ∀x∀y P(x,y) is false (the Week 2 example). Choosing x = 0 is not allowed because x is universally quantified.

questions.q: Which is equivalent to ¬∀x ∃y ∀z P(x, y, z)?
questions.explain: Move the ¬ across one quantifier at a time, flipping each one: ¬∀x → ∃x¬, ¬∃y → ∀y¬, ¬∀z → ∃z¬. Result: ∃x∀y∃z ¬P(x,y,z). Two common slips are flipping the quantifiers but forgetting to negate P, and negating P without flipping the quantifiers.

questions.q: Which is equivalent to ¬∃x ∀y (P(x, y) → Q(x, y))?
questions.explain: Flip both quantifiers (∃x∀y → ∀x∃y), then negate the conditional: ¬(P → Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q. Result: ∀x∃y(P(x,y) ∧ ¬Q(x,y)). Writing P → ¬Q is the usual mistake. The negation of a conditional is a conjunction.

questions.q: Which pair of statements is ALWAYS logically equivalent?
questions.explain: When the quantifiers are the same kind (both ∃ or both ∀), their order does not matter. When ∀ and ∃ are mixed, swapping them changes the meaning. For example, 'every San Martian likes some Austinite' is not the same as 'there is an Austinite every San Martian likes.'

questions.q: Domain: positive integers ℤ⁺. What is the truth value of ∃x ∀y (x ≤ y)?
choices: False; there is no largest positive integer
False; x ≤ y fails when y = x
questions.explain: We need one x that is ≤ every positive integer, and x = 1 works. The 'no largest integer' argument is about ∃x∀y(x ≥ y), which is a different statement. Choosing y = 1 is not allowed because y is universally quantified. (Over all of ℤ the statement would be false.)

questions.q: L(x, y) = 'x likes y', where x ranges over San Martians and y over Austinites. Translate ∀x ∃y L(x, y).
choices: Some San Martian likes every Austinite.
Every Austinite is liked by some San Martian.
Every San Martian likes some Austinite.
There is an Austinite whom every San Martian likes.
questions.explain: Read left to right: for each San Martian x, there exists an Austinite y (which may depend on x) that x likes. 'There is an Austinite whom every San Martian likes' is ∃y∀x L(x,y). That is a stronger claim, because one particular Austinite must work for everyone.

questions.q: Domain for x and y: {1, 2, 3}. Which statement is TRUE?
questions.explain: x = 1 satisfies 1 ≤ y for y = 1, 2, 3, so ∃x∀y(x ≤ y) is true. ∀x∃y(x < y) fails at x = 3 because nothing in the domain is bigger. ∃x∀y(x < y) fails because y = x gives x < x. ∀x∀y(x ≤ y) fails at x = 3, y = 1.

questions.q: Domain: all real numbers. Which formula correctly says 'every nonzero real number has a multiplicative inverse'?
questions.explain: Restrict x with a conditional: for all x, if x ≠ 0 then some y has xy = 1. ∀x∃y(xy = 1) leaves out the nonzero condition, so it is false at x = 0. ∃y∀x would need one y that is the inverse of every x. Using ∧ with ∀ makes the formula false at x = 0.

questions.q: L(x, y) = 'x loves y', domain: all people. Which is equivalent to 'Nobody loves everybody' (¬∃x ∀y L(x, y))?
questions.explain: Push the negation through: ¬∃x∀y L ≡ ∀x ¬∀y L ≡ ∀x∃y ¬L(x,y), meaning everyone has at least one person they do not love. ∀x∀y ¬L(x,y) says nobody loves anybody, which is far stronger. That is the over-negation trap.

questions.q: Domain for x and y: all integers. What is the truth value of ∀x ∃y (x = 2y)?
choices: False; for x = 1 no integer y works
False; for x = 0 no integer y works
questions.explain: For x = 1 we would need y = 1/2, which is not an integer, so the statement is false. 'y = x/2' only works for even x (or if the domain were the reals). x = 0 is not a counterexample, because y = 0 works.

questions.q: Suppose ∃x ∀y P(x, y) is true. Which statement must also be true?
questions.explain: If one x works for every y, then for each y that same x serves as the needed witness, so ∀y∃x P(x,y) holds. The converse direction is not guaranteed. ∀x∃y P(x,y) is tempting, but it talks about every x, while we only know about one particular x.

questions.q: 'If it snows, school closes. School did not close. Therefore, it did not snow.' Which rule of inference is used?
questions.explain: Form: p → q, ¬q ∴ ¬p, which is modus tollens. Modus ponens would be p → q, p ∴ q (affirming the hypothesis), the usual mix-up. Modus tollens works because p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p, followed by modus ponens.

questions.q: 'Sam is at the gym or at the library. Sam is not at the gym. Therefore, Sam is at the library.' Which rule is used?
questions.explain: Form: p ∨ q, ¬p ∴ q, which is disjunctive syllogism. Resolution needs two disjunctions (p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r). Addition goes the other way (p ∴ p ∨ q).

questions.q: 'If I wake up late, I miss the bus. If I miss the bus, I am late to class. Therefore, if I wake up late, I am late to class.' Which rule is used?
questions.explain: Form: p → q, q → r ∴ p → r, which chains conditionals (hypothetical syllogism). Modus ponens is tempting, but it would need the premise 'I woke up late' stated as a fact, and its conclusion would be a plain statement rather than a conditional.

questions.q: 'If it rained, the grass is wet. The grass is wet. Therefore, it rained.' This argument is:
choices: Invalid: the fallacy of affirming the conclusion
Invalid: the fallacy of denying the hypothesis
questions.explain: Form: p → q, q ∴ p. Knowing q does not force p (a sprinkler could have wet the grass), so the argument is invalid. This is affirming the conclusion. It looks like modus ponens, but modus ponens affirms the hypothesis p, not the conclusion q.

questions.q: 'If n is divisible by 4, then n is even. 6 is not divisible by 4. Therefore, 6 is not even.' This argument is:
choices: Invalid: the fallacy of affirming the conclusion
Invalid: the fallacy of denying the hypothesis
questions.explain: Form: p → q, ¬p ∴ ¬q. A false hypothesis tells us nothing about q, and indeed 6 is even. Modus tollens would need ¬q (not even) as the premise and would conclude ¬p, so the roles here are reversed.

questions.q: 'It is cold and sunny. Therefore, it is cold.' Which rule is used?
questions.explain: Form: p ∧ q ∴ p, which is simplification. Conjunction goes the other direction (p, q ∴ p ∧ q). Addition is p ∴ p ∨ q.

questions.q: 'Alex is a math major. Therefore, Alex is a math major or a computer science major.' Which rule is used?
questions.explain: Form: p ∴ p ∨ q. Since p is true, any disjunction containing p is true, which is the addition rule. Simplification is tempting because the argument feels like it 'drops' information, but simplification starts from a conjunction p ∧ q.

questions.q: 'Jasmine is skiing or it is not snowing. It is snowing or Bart is playing hockey. Therefore, Jasmine is skiing or Bart is playing hockey.' Which rule is used?
questions.explain: Let p = 'it is snowing.' The premises are (s ∨ ¬p) and (p ∨ h), and the conclusion is s ∨ h. This is resolution: p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r ∴ q ∨ r. Disjunctive syllogism would need ¬p stated outright as a separate premise.

questions.q: 'All CS majors take discrete math. Lee is a CS major. Therefore, Lee takes discrete math.' Which rule is used?
questions.explain: Form: ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)), P(a) ∴ Q(a). This is universal instantiation (to Lee) followed by modus ponens, combined into universal modus ponens. Universal modus tollens would start from ¬Q(a) and conclude ¬P(a).

questions.q: 'Every student in this class passed. Taylor did not pass. Therefore, Taylor is not a student in this class.' Which rule is used?
questions.explain: Form: ∀x(S(x) → P(x)), ¬P(t) ∴ ¬S(t). This is universal modus tollens, and it is valid. It is tempting to call it a fallacy, but it denies the CONCLUSION (¬P), which is valid. Denying the hypothesis would be ¬S(t) ∴ ¬P(t).

questions.q: 'Maria got an A on the exam. Therefore, someone got an A on the exam.' Which rule is used?
questions.explain: From P(c) for a particular c, conclude ∃x P(x): existential generalization. Universal generalization would require P(c) for an ARBITRARY c in order to conclude ∀x P(x), and one specific person is not enough for that. Instantiation goes the other direction, from a quantified statement to an instance.

questions.q: An argument with premises p₁, …, pₙ and conclusion c is a valid rule of inference exactly when:
questions.explain: View the rule as the conditional [Hypotheses] → Conclusion. It is a rule of inference when that conditional's truth table is a tautology, so whenever all hypotheses are true the conclusion is true. Requiring ↔ is too strong: the conclusion may be true even when the hypotheses are not.

questions.q: Premises: p → q, q → r, ¬r. What follows?
questions.explain: Hypothetical syllogism on p → q and q → r gives p → r. Modus tollens with ¬r then gives ¬p. (Equivalently: modus tollens on q → r gives ¬q, and again on p → q gives ¬p.) r directly contradicts the premise ¬r, and p or q would make r true.

questions.q: Which step in this argument is incorrectly justified?
questions.code:
1. p ∨ q      Premise
2. ¬p         Premise
3. q          Disjunctive syllogism (1, 2)
4. q → r      Premise
5. r          Modus tollens (3, 4)
choices: Step 5: it should be modus ponens
Step 5: it should be hypothetical syllogism
Step 3: it should be modus tollens
questions.explain: Step 3 is correct: p ∨ q and ¬p give q by disjunctive syllogism. Step 5 goes from q and q → r to r, which affirms the hypothesis: modus ponens, not modus tollens. Hypothetical syllogism would need two conditionals.

questions.q: To prove 'If 5n + 3 is odd, then n is even' by contraposition, what do you assume and what do you show?
choices: Assume n is even; show 5n + 3 is odd.
Assume 5n + 3 is odd; show n is even.
Assume n is odd; show 5n + 3 is even.
Assume 5n + 3 is odd and n is odd; derive a contradiction.
questions.explain: The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p: 'If n is odd, then 5n + 3 is even.' So assume ¬q (n odd) and show ¬p (5n + 3 even). Assuming 5n + 3 is odd is a direct proof. Assuming n is even proves the converse. The last choice is proof by contradiction.

questions.q: To prove 'If n² is odd, then n is odd' by contradiction, what do you assume?
choices: n² is odd and n is even
n is odd, and then show n² is odd
n² is even and n is odd
questions.explain: To prove p → q by contradiction, assume p ∧ ¬q (the hypothesis AND the negated conclusion) and derive a contradiction. Here: n² is odd and n is even. Assuming only 'n is even' is the start of a contraposition proof. Forgetting to keep the hypothesis p is the usual slip.

questions.q: To prove 'If xy is odd, then x is odd and y is odd' by contradiction, what are all the assumptions?
choices: xy is even, and x is odd and y is odd
xy is odd, and x is even or y is even
x is even or y is even
xy is odd, and x is even and y is even
questions.explain: Assume p ∧ ¬q, where p = 'xy odd' and q = 'x odd ∧ y odd.' By De Morgan, ¬q = 'x even OR y even.' Writing 'x even AND y even' is the classic De Morgan error (compare Assignment 3: ¬(a = 0 or b = 0) is a ≠ 0 and b ≠ 0). The last choice drops the hypothesis entirely.

questions.q: In a direct proof that the sum of two odd integers m and n is even, which is the best continuation?
choices: Write m = 2k + 1 and n = 2k + 1; then m + n = 4k + 2 = 2(2k + 1).
Note that 3 + 5 = 8 and 7 + 9 = 16 are even, so the claim holds.
Write m = 2k + 1 and n = 2l + 1; then m + n = 2(k + l) + 1.
Write m = 2k + 1 and n = 2l + 1; then m + n = 2(k + l + 1), where k + l + 1 is an integer.
questions.explain: Use different variables for different integers: m + n = 2k + 2l + 2 = 2(k + l + 1), which is even by definition. Reusing k silently assumes m = n ('don't reuse variable names'). Examples are not proofs. The last choice makes an arithmetic error.

questions.q: What is wrong with this 'proof' that the sum of two even integers is a multiple of 4?
questions.code:
Claim: If m and n are even, then m + n is a multiple of 4.
Proof: Since m and n are even, m = 2k and n = 2k.
Then m + n = 4k, a multiple of 4.
choices: It reuses the variable k, which wrongly forces m = n.
Even integers should be written as 2k + 1.
It should have been a proof by contradiction.
Nothing; the claim is true and the proof is valid.
questions.explain: m and n are arbitrary, so they need separate witnesses: m = 2k, n = 2l, and m + n = 2(k + l), which is only guaranteed to be even. Reusing k quietly assumes m = n. The claim itself is false (2 + 4 = 6 is not a multiple of 4), so the proof cannot be valid.

questions.q: In the proof that n odd implies n² odd: n = 2k + 1, so n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(___) + 1. What fills the blank?
questions.explain: 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, and 2k² + 2k is an integer, so n² is odd by definition (Assignment 3). 4k² + 4k forgets to factor out the 2, and k² + k divides out one 2 too many.

questions.q: 'If n is a positive integer and n² < 0, then n = 5.' Which proof method applies most directly?
questions.explain: The hypothesis 'n² < 0' is never true for a positive integer, so p → q is vacuously true: show p is false. A trivial proof would instead show the conclusion q is always true, which is not the case here (n = 5 is not always true).

questions.q: 'If n is an integer greater than 10, then n² ≥ 0.' Which proof method applies most directly?
questions.explain: The conclusion n² ≥ 0 is true for every integer, so p → q holds no matter what p is. Showing that q is true is a trivial proof. A vacuous proof would require the hypothesis to be false, but 'n > 10' is true for many integers.

questions.q: Which value is a counterexample to 'Every odd integer greater than 1 is prime'?
questions.explain: A counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis (odd and > 1) and fail the conclusion (be prime). 9 = 3·3 is odd and not prime. 3 and 7 are prime. 2 is not odd, so it is not even in the scope of the claim.

questions.q: In the proof by contradiction that √2 is irrational, what is assumed at the start?
choices: √2 = m/n where m and n are both even
√2 = m/n for integers m, n with n ≠ 0 and no common factors
m² = 2n² for some odd integer m
questions.explain: Assume the negation of the claim: √2 is rational, written in lowest terms as m/n. The proof then shows that m and n are both even, which contradicts 'no common factors.' Assuming 'both even' at the start would assume the conclusion of the argument. Assuming √2 is irrational assumes what we want to prove.

questions.q: By the pigeonhole principle, what is the minimum number of people needed to guarantee that at least two were born in the same month?
questions.explain: With 12 months as boxes, 12 people could each have a different month. The (k + 1)-st person forces a repeat, so 13 people guarantee a shared month. Answering 12 is the off-by-one error: you need one more pigeon than boxes.

questions.q: Proving 'if n is even and m is odd, then mn is even': with n = 2k and m = 2l + 1, mn = 2(___). What fills the blank?
questions.explain: mn = (2l + 1)(2k) = 4kl + 2k = 2(2kl + k), and 2kl + k is an integer, so mn is even (Week 3 example). 4kl + 2k is the product before factoring out the 2. kl + k divides by 2 twice.

questions.q: Which proof technique proves p → q by assuming p ∧ ¬q and deriving a contradiction?
questions.explain: Proof by contradiction for a conditional assumes the hypothesis together with the negated conclusion, then derives something impossible. Contraposition is different: it assumes only ¬q and directly derives ¬p, with no contradiction needed.

questions.q: What is the flaw in this attempted proof?
questions.code:
Claim: If n² is even, then n is even.
Proof: Assume n is even, so n = 2k for some integer k.
Then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²), so n² is even. ∎
choices: It uses an example instead of a general argument.
Even integers must be written as 2k + 1.
It proves the converse, 'if n is even then n² is even,' not the claim.
questions.explain: The claim is 'n² even → n even,' but the proof assumes n is even and concludes n² is even, which is the converse q → p. A correct approach is contraposition: assume n is odd and show n² is odd. The algebra itself is fine and uses an arbitrary k, not an example.

questions.q: Write {x ∈ ℤ | x² < 10} using the roster method.
questions.explain: Integers with x² < 10: 0 (0), ±1 (1), ±2 (4), ±3 (9). ±4 gives 16, which is too big. Forgetting the negative integers (giving {0, 1, 2, 3}) is the most common error, since x² < 10 holds for −3 as well.

questions.q: Using this course's convention, which set is ℕ (the natural numbers)?
questions.explain: In this course, ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …}, the nonnegative integers. {1, 2, 3, …} is ℤ⁺ (positive integers), which is easy to confuse with ℕ. The third set is ℤ and the last is ℚ.

questions.q: What is |{a, b, a, c, b}|?
questions.explain: Repetition in a set is ignored, so {a, b, a, c, b} = {a, b, c}, which has cardinality 3. Answering 5 counts the listed symbols instead of the distinct elements.

questions.q: Which statement is true?
questions.explain: The empty set is a subset of every set (theorem from class), so ∅ ⊆ {1, 2}. But ∅ is not an ELEMENT of {1, 2}, since its elements are just 1 and 2. {1} ⊆ {1, 2} would be true, but {1} ∈ {1, 2} is false. '1 ⊆ …' is meaningless because 1 is not a set.

questions.q: Let S = {∅, {∅}}. Which statement is correct?
questions.explain: {∅} is listed as an element of S, so {∅} ∈ S. The only element of {∅} is ∅, and ∅ ∈ S, so {∅} ⊆ S as well. Both relations hold. |S| = 2 because ∅ and {∅} are different objects.

Count the top-level elements: ∅, {∅}, and {∅, {∅}}, which gives 3. The 'empty' look of the elements is a trap: ∅ is still an element here, and nested braces count as one element each. Answering 4 counts elements inside the inner sets.

questions.q: Let A = {1, 2} and B = {1, 2, 3}. Which statement is true?
questions.explain: Every element of A is in B and A ≠ B, so A is a proper subset: A ⊂ B. B ⊄ A because 3 ∉ A. A ∈ B would require the set {1, 2} itself to be listed as an element of B, which it is not. Confusing ∈ with ⊆ is the common error.

questions.q: What is the standard way to prove A ⊆ B?
choices: Let x ∈ B be arbitrary and show x ∈ A.
Find one element of A that is also in B.
Let x ∈ A be arbitrary and show x ∈ B.
questions.explain: A ⊆ B means ∀x(x ∈ A → x ∈ B), so take an arbitrary element of A and show it lies in B. Starting from x ∈ B proves the reverse inclusion. One example proves nothing about all elements, and comparing sizes does not show containment.

questions.q: How do you prove two sets A and B are equal?
choices: Show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
questions.explain: Sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements, which is equivalent to mutual inclusion. Equal cardinality is not enough ({1} and {2} both have size 1). One inclusion only gives a subset relation.

questions.q: Which set is equal to {1, 2, 3}?
questions.explain: Order and repetition do not matter, so {3, 2, 1, 1} = {1, 2, 3}. {1, {2, 3}} has two elements, one of which is a set. {{1, 2, 3}} has a single element (the whole set). {0, 1, 2, 3} has an extra element.

questions.q: Which number is an element of ℚ but NOT of ℤ?
questions.explain: −0.75 = −3/4 is a ratio of integers, so it is in ℚ, and it is not an integer. −3 is in both ℚ and ℤ. √2 and π are irrational, so they are not in ℚ at all.

questions.q: Write {x ∈ ℤ⁺ | x divides 12} using the roster method.
questions.explain: The positive divisors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The usual omissions are 1 and 12 themselves, which are divisors too. 0 is excluded because it is not in ℤ⁺ (and 0 does not divide 12).

questions.q: Which statement about ∅ and {∅} is correct?
questions.explain: ∅ has no elements. {∅} is a set with one element, namely the empty set, so they are different sets with cardinalities 0 and 1. ∅ ∈ ∅ is false because the empty set contains nothing. Think of {∅} as an empty box inside a box.

questions.q: What is P({a, b})?
questions.explain: The power set contains every subset, including ∅ and the set itself: 2² = 4 subsets. Omitting ∅ or {a, b} is the usual error. Writing a instead of {a} confuses an element with the subset containing it.

questions.q: If |S| = 13, what is |P(S)|?
questions.explain: |P(S)| = 2ⁿ, so 2¹³ = 8192 (Assignment 3). 169 = 13² and 26 = 2·13 are the usual formula mix-ups. 4096 = 2¹² is an off-by-one in the exponent.

questions.q: Let S = {a, {a}}. What is P(S)?
questions.explain: S has two distinct elements, a and {a}, so P(S) has 2² = 4 subsets: ∅, {a}, {{a}}, and S itself (Week 4). The easy slip is to skip {{a}}, the subset containing only the element {a}. Listing bare a confuses elements with subsets.

questions.q: What is P({∅})?
questions.explain: {∅} has one element (∅), so it has 2¹ = 2 subsets: the empty subset ∅ and the whole set {∅}. Therefore P({∅}) = {∅, {∅}}. Answering {∅} forgets that the set itself is one of its subsets.

questions.q: What is |P(P({1}))|?
questions.explain: P({1}) = {∅, {1}} has 2 elements, so P(P({1})) has 2² = 4 elements. Answering 2 stops after one power set. 16 = 2⁴ applies the power set a third time.

questions.q: What is |P(∅)|?
questions.explain: The empty set has exactly one subset, itself, so P(∅) = {∅} and |P(∅)| = 2⁰ = 1. Answering 0 confuses P(∅) = {∅} with ∅.

questions.q: How many subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} contain the element 1?
questions.explain: Every such subset includes 1, and each of the other 4 elements is freely in or out: 2⁴ = 16. 32 = 2⁵ counts all subsets. Exactly half of the subsets contain any given element.

questions.q: How many PROPER subsets does a 4-element set have?
questions.explain: A 4-element set has 2⁴ = 16 subsets. A proper subset excludes only the set itself, leaving 16 − 1 = 15. (∅ IS a proper subset.) 14 comes from also wrongly excluding ∅.

questions.q: Which of these is an element of P({1, 2, 3})?
questions.explain: Elements of P(A) are subsets of A. {1, 3} ⊆ {1, 2, 3}, so it qualifies. 2 is an element of A, not a subset of it. {4} is not a subset because 4 ∉ A. {{1}} would require {1} to be an element of A.

questions.q: If |P(A)| = 64, what is |A|?
questions.explain: |P(A)| = 2^|A| = 64 = 2⁶, so |A| = 6. Answering 8 takes the square root (8² = 64), confusing 2ⁿ with n².

questions.q: Which statement is true for EVERY set S?
questions.explain: ∅ and S are always subsets of S, so both are elements of P(S). S ⊆ P(S) fails in general: for S = {1}, 1 ∉ P(S) = {∅, {1}}. The cardinality is 2^|S|, not 2|S|.

questions.q: Let A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y, z}. Which is an element of A × B?
questions.explain: A × B = {(a, b) | a ∈ A, b ∈ B} contains ordered pairs with the first coordinate from A and the second from B. (x, 2) has the order reversed, so it belongs to B × A. {2, x} is a set, not an ordered pair.

questions.q: What is |{x ∈ ℤ | x² < 20}|?
questions.explain: The set is {−4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4} (Assignment 3), since 4² = 16 < 20 but 5² = 25. That is 9 elements. 5 counts only {0, …, 4}, and 8 forgets 0.
A − B = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B}: remove 3 and 5 from A, leaving {1, 7, 9}. {4, 6} is B − A, the common mix-up (in general A − B ≠ B − A). {3, 5} is A ∩ B.

questions.q: U = {1, 2, …, 10}, A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}, B = {1, 2, 3, 4}. What is the complement of A ∪ B?
questions.explain: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10}, so (A ∪ B)′ = U − (A ∪ B) = {5, 7, 9}. Check with De Morgan: A′ ∩ B′ = {1,3,5,7,9} ∩ {5,…,10} = {5, 7, 9}. The last choice is A′ ∪ B′, which complements each set but forgets to flip ∪ to ∩.

questions.q: Of 200 students, 120 take Spanish, 85 take French, and 30 take neither. How many take both?
questions.explain: |S ∪ F| = 200 − 30 = 170. Inclusion–exclusion: |S ∪ F| = |S| + |F| − |S ∩ F|, so 170 = 205 − |S ∩ F| and |S ∩ F| = 35. Answering 5 (205 − 200) forgets to remove the 30 students who take neither.

questions.q: |A| = 10, |B| = 15, and |A ∩ B| = 4. What is |A ∪ B|?
questions.explain: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| = 10 + 15 − 4 = 21. Answering 25 just adds, double-counting the 4 shared elements. 29 adds the intersection instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: By De Morgan's law for sets, (A ∩ B)′ equals:
questions.explain: Complementing flips ∩ to ∪ and complements each set: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. This mirrors ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q. A′ ∩ B′ is (A ∪ B)′, the other De Morgan law.

questions.q: Let A_i = {i, i + 1, i + 2} for i = 1, 2, 3. What is A₁ ∩ A₂ ∩ A₃?
questions.explain: A₁ = {1,2,3}, A₂ = {2,3,4}, A₃ = {3,4,5}. The only element common to all three is 3. {1, …, 5} is the union. {1, 2, 3} is just A₁.

questions.q: Let A_i = {x ∈ ℤ | x ≥ i} for i = 1, 2, 3, …. What is the intersection of all the A_i (i = 1 to ∞)?
questions.explain: An integer n lies in A_i only when i ≤ n, so n ∉ A_{n+1}. No integer is in every A_i, so the intersection is empty. ℤ⁺ is the union of the A_i, which is the common mix-up.

questions.q: Proof that A′ ∩ B′ ⊆ (A ∪ B)′: 'Let x ∈ A′ ∩ B′. Then x ∈ A′ and x ∈ B′, so x ∉ A and x ∉ B. Hence ______. Therefore x ∈ (A ∪ B)′.' What fills the blank?
questions.explain: Since x is in neither A nor B, it is not in their union, and by the definition of complement x ∈ (A ∪ B)′. 'x ∉ A ∩ B' is true but too weak: it does not lead to x ∈ (A ∪ B)′. The same goes for x ∈ A′ ∪ B′.

questions.q: Which pair of sets is disjoint?
questions.explain: Disjoint means A ∩ B = ∅. {1, 3, 5} ∩ {2, 4, 6} = ∅. Each of the other pairs shares an element (2, b, and 0 respectively).

questions.q: Which set always equals A − B?
questions.explain: A − B = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B} = A ∩ B′. A′ ∩ B is B − A, the reversed difference. (A ∪ B)′ contains elements of neither set.

questions.q: A = {a, b, c, d} and B = {c, d, e}. What is (A − B) ∪ (B − A)?
questions.explain: A − B = {a, b} and B − A = {e}, so the union is {a, b, e}: the elements in exactly one of the sets. {c, d} is A ∩ B. {a, b} forgets B − A.

questions.q: Simplify A ∪ (A ∩ B).
questions.explain: Absorption law: every element of A ∩ B is already in A, so adding them to A changes nothing, and A ∪ (A ∩ B) = A. This parallels p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p in propositional logic. A ∪ B is the tempting guess.

questions.q: With universal set U = ℝ, which number belongs to ℚ′ (the complement of ℚ)?
questions.explain: The complement of ℚ within ℝ is the set of irrational numbers. √2 is irrational. 22/7 is tempting because it approximates π, but it is a ratio of integers and therefore rational. 0.5 and −7 are rational as well.
B ∪ C = {2, 3, 4, 5}, and intersecting with A gives {2, 3}. Equivalently, (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) = {2, 3} ∪ {3} by the distributive law. {2, 3, 4, 5} is (A ∩ B) ∪ C, which ignores the parentheses.

questions.q: f: ℤ → ℤ, f(x) = x². What is the range of f?
questions.explain: The range is the set of actual images: the perfect squares 0, 1, 4, 9, …. ℤ is the codomain, and confusing codomain with range is the usual error. ℕ includes non-squares like 2, and {1, 4, 9, …} forgets f(0) = 0.

questions.q: A = {a, b, c}, B = {1, 2, 3}. Which assignment is NOT a function from A to B?
questions.explain: A function assigns each element of A exactly one element of B. The first assignment gives a two images. Sending everything to 1 is still a function (a constant function), and two inputs sharing an output is allowed.

questions.q: f: ℤ → ℤ, f(x) = ⌊x/2⌋. Which describes f?
questions.explain: Not one-to-one: f(0) = ⌊0⌋ = 0 and f(1) = ⌊1/2⌋ = 0. Onto: for any integer y, f(2y) = y. Students often see the division by 2 and assume some outputs are skipped, but every integer is hit.

questions.q: f: ℤ × ℤ → ℤ, f(m, n) = 2m − n. To show f is onto, which input maps to an arbitrary z ∈ ℤ?
questions.explain: f(0, −z) = 2·0 − (−z) = z, so every integer is an image (homework). f(z, 0) = 2z and f(0, z) = −z miss the target. (z/2, 0) is not in ℤ × ℤ when z is odd.

questions.q: f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = 3x − 7. Which describes f?
questions.explain: One-to-one: 3x − 7 = 3y − 7 implies x = y. Onto: for any y, x = (y + 7)/3 is real and f(x) = y. So f is a bijection. Over ℤ it would not be onto, but over ℝ the division is always allowed.

questions.q: f: ℤ → ℤ, f(x) = 2x + 1. Which describes f?
questions.explain: 2x + 1 = 2y + 1 implies x = y, so f is one-to-one. Every output is odd, so even integers like 0 have no preimage and f is not onto. Calling it a bijection is the common slip, since the same formula over ℝ would be one.

questions.q: f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x². Which describes f?
questions.explain: Not one-to-one: f(1) = f(−1). Not onto: −1 has no real preimage. Students often catch one failure but not the other.

questions.q: f: ℤ⁺ → ℤ⁺, f(x) = x². Which describes f?
questions.explain: With a positive domain, x² = y² gives (x − y)(x + y) = 0, and x + y > 0, so x = y: one-to-one (lecture proof). It is not onto because 2 is not a perfect square. Restricting the domain fixed injectivity but not surjectivity.

questions.q: |A| = 5 and |B| = 3. Which statement about a function f: A → B must be true?
questions.explain: If f is one-to-one then |A| ≤ |B|, and 5 > 3, so two elements of A must share an image (pigeonhole). f could be onto (|A| ≥ |B| allows it) but need not be, for example a constant function. A bijection needs |A| = |B|.

questions.q: Which is the correct start of a proof that f: A → B is one-to-one?
choices: Let x, y ∈ A and assume f(x) = f(y); show x = y.
Let b ∈ B; find a ∈ A with f(a) = b.
Let x, y ∈ A and assume x = y; show f(x) = f(y).
questions.explain: Injective means f(x) = f(y) implies x = y, so assume equal outputs and derive equal inputs. The reversed version (x = y ⇒ f(x) = f(y)) holds for every function and proves nothing. Finding preimages proves onto. One example is not a proof.
The image of a subset S is f(S) = {f(s) | s ∈ S} = {f(a), f(b), f(c)} = {1, 2, 1} = {1, 2}. {1, 2, 3} is the range of all of f (it includes f(d)). {1, 2, 3, 4} is the codomain.

questions.q: Same f: {a, b, c, d} → {1, 2, 3, 4} with f(a) = 1, f(b) = 2, f(c) = 1, f(d) = 3. What is the range, and is f onto?
choices: Range {1, 2, 3}; not onto, since 4 has no preimage
Range {a, b, c, d}; not onto
Range {1, 2, 3}; onto, because every element of A is used
questions.explain: The range is the set of actual outputs, {1, 2, 3}. Onto requires every element of the codomain to be hit, and 4 is missed. Using every element of the domain is required of every function and says nothing about onto.

questions.q: f: ℤ × ℤ → ℤ, f(m, n) = m + n. Which pair of inputs shows that f is NOT one-to-one?
questions.explain: (1, 0) ≠ (0, 1) but f(1, 0) = f(0, 1) = 1: different inputs, same output. (1,1) and (2,2) give different outputs (2 and 4), as do (1,2) and (2,3). A pair of identical inputs shows nothing. (The lecture showed f is onto via f(y, 0) = y.)

questions.q: f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = 3x + 2 on ℝ. What is (f ∘ g)(x)?
questions.explain: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = 2(3x + 2) + 3 = 6x + 7. 6x + 11 is (g ∘ f)(x) = 3(2x + 3) + 2, from applying the functions in the wrong order. In general f ∘ g ≠ g ∘ f. The last choice multiplies f(x)·g(x).

questions.q: f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 4 on ℝ. What is (g ∘ f)(−3)?
questions.explain: (g ∘ f)(−3) = g(f(−3)) = g(9) = 13. Answering 1 computes (f ∘ g)(−3) = f(1) = 1, which applies g first. −5 comes from treating (−3)² as −9.

questions.q: f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = 3x − 7. What is f⁻¹(y)?
questions.explain: Solve y = 3x − 7 for x: x = (y + 7)/3. Check: f((y + 7)/3) = y + 7 − 7 = y. 1/(3y − 7) confuses the inverse function with the reciprocal. (y − 7)/3 undoes the steps without reversing the operations.

questions.q: Why is f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x² not invertible?
choices: It is not defined for negative x.
It is one-to-one, but its range is all of ℝ.
It is not a bijection; for example f(2) = f(−2) = 4.
Its inverse would be √x, which is a function on ℝ.
questions.explain: Only bijections have inverses. Since f(2) = f(−2), 'f⁻¹(4)' would need two values (and negative numbers have no preimage at all). f is defined for all real x. √x is not defined on all of ℝ and only returns nonnegative values.

questions.q: What is ⌊−4.3⌋?
questions.explain: ⌊x⌋ is the largest integer ≤ x. Since −5 ≤ −4.3 < −4, ⌊−4.3⌋ = −5. Answering −4 is the classic error of 'chopping off the decimal,' which rounds toward zero instead of down.

⌈4.2⌉ = 5 (smallest integer ≥ 4.2) and ⌊−2.7⌋ = −3 (largest integer ≤ −2.7), so 5 − (−3) = 8. Truncating both (4 − (−2)) gives 6. Getting only one of the two right gives 7. Dropping the minus sign gives 5 − 3 = 2.

questions.q: For which real numbers x is ⌈x⌉ − ⌊x⌋ = 1?
choices: Exactly when x is an integer
Exactly when x is not an integer
questions.explain: If x is an integer, ⌈x⌉ = ⌊x⌋ = x and the difference is 0. Otherwise x lies strictly between two consecutive integers, so ceiling and floor differ by 1. The sign of x does not matter.

questions.q: Data is stored in bytes of 8 bits. How many bytes are needed to store 100 bits?
questions.explain: We need the smallest whole number of bytes with 8·b ≥ 100: b = ⌈100/8⌉ = ⌈12.5⌉ = 13. Using the floor (12) would leave 4 bits unstored, and a fractional byte is impossible.

questions.q: f: ℤ → ℤ, f(x) = ⌊x/2⌋. What is f(−7)?
questions.explain: −7/2 = −3.5 and ⌊−3.5⌋ = −4, the largest integer ≤ −3.5. −3 rounds toward zero, the usual mistake with negative floors. −3.5 is not an integer and so is not in the codomain ℤ.

questions.q: f: {1, 2, 3} → {a, b, c} is the bijection f(1) = c, f(2) = a, f(3) = b. What is f⁻¹(a)?
questions.explain: f⁻¹(b) = a exactly when f(a) = b, i.e. you reverse the assignments. Since f(2) = a, f⁻¹(a) = 2. Answering c computes f(1) instead of inverting.

questions.q: f: {1, 2, 3} → {a, b, c} with f(1) = b, f(2) = c, f(3) = a, and g: {a, b, c} → {x, y} with g(a) = y, g(b) = x, g(c) = x. What is g ∘ f?
choices: Undefined, because only f ∘ g makes sense
questions.explain: (g ∘ f)(n) = g(f(n)): g(f(1)) = g(b) = x, g(f(2)) = g(c) = x, g(f(3)) = g(a) = y. The second choice applies g to a, b, c in alphabetical order instead of to f's outputs. g ∘ f is defined because f's codomain is g's domain. It is f ∘ g that is undefined here.

questions.q: If f: A → B is a bijection, what is f⁻¹ ∘ f?
questions.explain: (f⁻¹ ∘ f)(a) = f⁻¹(f(a)) = a for every a ∈ A, so it is ι_A. f ∘ f⁻¹ is the identity on B, and mixing up which side is which is the common slip. Track where the composite starts: f⁻¹ ∘ f takes inputs from A.

questions.q: f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x³ + 1. What is f⁻¹(y)?
questions.explain: Solve y = x³ + 1: x³ = y − 1, so x = ∛(y − 1). ∛y − 1 undoes the operations in the wrong order: the +1 was applied last, so it must be undone first. Check: (∛(y − 1))³ + 1 = y.

questions.q: a_n = 5 + 3ⁿ for n ≥ 0. What are a₀, a₁, a₂?
questions.explain: a₀ = 5 + 3⁰ = 6, a₁ = 5 + 3 = 8, a₂ = 5 + 9 = 14. Writing 5 for a₀ treats 3⁰ as 0, but 3⁰ = 1. 8, 14, 32 are a₁, a₂, a₃, which is off by one in the index.

questions.q: a_k = a_{k−1} + 3a_{k−2} with a₀ = 1 and a₁ = 2. What is a₄?
questions.explain: a₂ = a₁ + 3a₀ = 2 + 3 = 5. a₃ = a₂ + 3a₁ = 5 + 6 = 11. a₄ = a₃ + 3a₂ = 11 + 15 = 26. 11 is a₃, stopping one step early. 76 comes from putting the 3 on a_{k−1} instead (3a_{k−1} + a_{k−2}).

questions.q: Fibonacci: F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1, F_n = F_{n−1} + F_{n−2}. What is F₇?
questions.explain: The sequence is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 for F₀ through F₇, so F₇ = 13. 8 is F₆, which comes from starting the count at 1 instead of 0. 21 is F₈.

questions.q: The arithmetic progression (a_n) = (5 − 3n), n ≥ 0, has initial term a and common difference d equal to:
questions.explain: An arithmetic progression has the form a + dn. Here a₀ = 5 and each step subtracts 3, so d = −3. a = 2 is a₁, which is what you get by starting at n = 1. d = 3 drops the sign.

questions.q: Which formula (n ≥ 0) gives the geometric progression 3, −6, 12, −24, …?
questions.explain: A geometric progression has the form a·rⁿ. The initial term is a = 3 and the ratio is −6/3 = −2, so a_n = 3(−2)ⁿ. 3·2ⁿ misses the alternating sign. −2·3ⁿ swaps a and r, giving −2, −6, ….

questions.q: The arithmetic sequence a₀ = 2, a₁ = 7, a₂ = 12, … has a_10 = ?
questions.explain: a_n = 2 + 5n, so a₁₀ = 2 + 50 = 52. 47 = a₉ is the off-by-one from treating a₁₀ as the 10th term listed. Because the index starts at 0, a₁₀ is the 11th term.

questions.q: a_n = n·a_{n−1} with a₀ = 1. What is a₅?
questions.explain: a₁ = 1, a₂ = 2, a₃ = 6, a₄ = 24, a₅ = 5·24 = 120, so a_n = n!. 24 = a₄ is one step short. 15 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 adds where it should multiply.

questions.q: Which recurrence and initial condition generate 2, 6, 18, 54, … (starting at a₀)?
questions.explain: Each term is 3 times the previous one, and the first term is 2. a_n = a_{n−1} + 4 gives 2, 6, 10, … (it only matches the first two terms). a_n = 3a_{n−1} with a₀ = 6 has the right rule but the wrong initial condition, since it starts at 6.

questions.q: Find a closed formula for a_n = a_{n−1} + 5 with a₀ = 3.
questions.explain: Each step adds 5, so this is an arithmetic progression with initial term 3 and difference 5: a_n = 3 + 5n. 3 + 5(n − 1) would fit only if indexing started at n = 1. 3·5ⁿ is geometric (it multiplies instead of adding).

questions.q: a_n = (−1)ⁿ(n + 1). What is a₃?
questions.explain: a₃ = (−1)³(3 + 1) = −1·4 = −4. 4 forgets that an odd power of −1 is −1. ±3 forgets the +1.

questions.q: Which expression equals 6!?
questions.explain: n! = n·(n − 1)!, so 6! = 6·5! = 720 (compare 4!·5 = 5! in lecture). 6·5·4 = 120 stops multiplying too early. 5·6! = 3600, and 5! + 6 = 126.

questions.q: a_n = n!/(n − 2)! for n ≥ 2. What is a₅?
questions.explain: 5!/3! = (5·4·3!)/3! = 5·4 = 20. 60 = 5!/2! comes from using (n − 3)! in the denominator. 6 = 3! comes from writing down only the denominator.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=1}^{4} (k² − k).
questions.explain: Terms: 0 + 2 + 6 + 12 = 20. Equivalently, Σk² − Σk = 30 − 10 = 20. 30 is just Σk² (forgetting to subtract), and 10 is just Σk.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=3}^{5} (1/2)^k.
questions.explain: 1/8 + 1/16 + 1/32 = 4/32 + 2/32 + 1/32 = 7/32 (lecture example). 15/32 starts the sum at k = 2 instead of 3. 31/32 starts at k = 1.

questions.q: Using Σ_{k=1}^{n} k² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, evaluate Σ_{k=1}^{50} k².
questions.explain: 50·51·101/6 = 257550/6 = 42925. 1275 = 50·51/2 is Σk, from using the wrong formula. 40425 = 49·50·99/6 is an off-by-one (n = 49). 2500 = 50² is just the last term.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=11}^{20} k.
questions.explain: Σ_{k=11}^{20} k = Σ_{1}^{20} − Σ_{1}^{10} = 210 − 55 = 155. 144 = 210 − 66 subtracts up to 11, which removes the k = 11 term that should be included. 165 = 210 − 45 subtracts only up to 9.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=10}^{20} k².
questions.explain: Σ_{1}^{20} k² = 20·21·41/6 = 2870 and Σ_{1}^{9} k² = 9·10·19/6 = 285, so the sum is 2870 − 285 = 2585. 2485 = 2870 − 385 subtracts Σ_{1}^{10}, which wrongly removes the k = 10 term. As in lecture (Σ_{50}^{100} = Σ_{1}^{100} − Σ_{1}^{49}), subtract up to one below the starting index.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=0}^{5} 3·2^k.

questions.explain: For |r| < 1, Σ_{k=0}^{∞} a·r^k = a/(1 − r) = 5/(2/3) = 15/2. 5/2 is the value of the sum starting at k = 1, which drops the first term 5.

questions.q: Evaluate the double sum Σ_{i=1}^{2} Σ_{j=1}^{3} (i + j).
questions.explain: Work inside-out. For fixed i, Σ_{j=1}^{3}(i + j) = 3i + 6. Then i = 1 gives 9 and i = 2 gives 12, for a total of 21. 18 is the lecture's Σ Σ i·j, which multiplies instead of adding.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=1}^{20} (3k − 2).
questions.explain: Split: 3Σk − Σ2 = 3·210 − 2·20 = 630 − 40 = 590. 628 subtracts 2 only once instead of 20 times (the constant is summed over all 20 terms).

questions.q: Which re-indexing is correct? Σ_{k=5}^{12} a_k = ?
questions.explain: Let j = k − 4. Then k = 5 → j = 1 and k = 12 → j = 8, and a_k = a_{j+4}. The sum has 12 − 5 + 1 = 8 terms. An upper limit of 7 drops a term. a_{j−4} shifts in the wrong direction.

questions.q: Which is a closed form for Σ_{k=1}^{n} (2k − 1), the sum of the first n odd numbers?
questions.explain: 2Σk − Σ1 = 2·n(n+1)/2 − n = n² + n − n = n². Check with n = 3: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9. n(n + 1) − 1 subtracts 1 once instead of n times.

questions.q: How many terms are in Σ_{k=7}^{30} a_k?
questions.explain: From m to n there are n − m + 1 terms: 30 − 7 + 1 = 24. 23 is the off-by-one fencepost error.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=0}^{100} 4.
questions.explain: The summand does not depend on k, so the sum is 4 × (number of terms) = 4 × 101 = 404, since k = 0 through 100 is 101 terms. 400 forgets the k = 0 term. 20200 treats the summand as 4k.

questions.q: Using Σ_{k=1}^{n} k³ = n²(n+1)²/4, evaluate Σ_{k=1}^{10} k³.
questions.explain: 10²·11²/4 = 100·121/4 = 3025 (which equals (Σk)² = 55²). 385 is Σk² and 55 is Σk, so both use the wrong power formula. 1000 is just the last term, 10³.

questions.q: Which divisibility statement is true?
questions.explain: a | b means b = a·m for some integer m. 0 = 3·0, so 3 | 0 (in fact every nonzero n divides 0). 0 | 3 is undefined/false because the divisor must be nonzero. 21 = 5m has no integer solution. 21 | 7 reverses the roles: 7 | 21 is true, but 21 does not divide 7.

questions.q: What are −23 div 5 and −23 mod 5?
questions.explain: The division algorithm requires 0 ≤ r < d: −23 = 5·(−5) + 2, so div = −5 and mod = 2. −4 and −3 satisfy −23 = 5(−4) − 3, but the remainder can't be negative. As in lecture, −17 div 3 = −6 and −17 mod 3 = 1.

questions.q: What are 145 div 12 and 145 mod 12?
questions.explain: 145 = 12·12 + 1 with 0 ≤ 1 < 12. q = 11, r = 13 satisfies 145 = 12·11 + 13, but a remainder of 13 is not less than 12.

questions.q: Suppose 4 | m and m | n. Which statement must be true?
questions.explain: Transitivity: m = 4k and n = m·l = 4(kl), so 4 | n. Nothing forces m = 4 (for example m = 12). With m = 4, n = 4 we have 8 ∤ n, so 8 | n is not guaranteed. n | 4 reverses the relation.

questions.q: Suppose 7 | x and 7 | y. Which must 7 also divide?
questions.explain: If a | b then a | bm, and if a | b and a | c then a | (b + c). So 7 | 3x and 7 | (−5y), giving 7 | 3x − 5y. Each other choice adds a constant that is not a multiple of 7, which breaks divisibility (try x = y = 7).

questions.q: Which expression is a proposition rather than a number?
questions.explain: a | b ('a divides b') is a statement that is either true or false, not an arithmetic operation. Here it is true since 30 = 6·5. 30/6, 30 mod 6, and 30 div 6 are numbers (5, 0, and 5). The vertical bar is easily mistaken for division.

questions.q: How many positive integers less than or equal to 100 are divisible by 7?
questions.explain: The multiples are 7·1, 7·2, …, 7·k with 7k ≤ 100, so k ≤ 100/7 ≈ 14.29 and the count is ⌊100/7⌋ = 14 (the last one is 98). Rounding 14.29 up to 15 is the error: 105 > 100.

questions.q: Which value could n mod 8 have?
questions.explain: By the division algorithm, n mod d is the remainder r with 0 ≤ r < d, so n mod 8 ∈ {0, 1, …, 7}. 8 is not allowed because the remainder must be strictly less than the divisor. Negative remainders are not allowed either.

questions.q: What is −1 mod 7?
questions.explain: −1 = 7·(−1) + 6 with 0 ≤ 6 < 7, so −1 mod 7 = 6. On the 'clock' with 7 hours, one step back from 0 lands on 6. Answering −1 or 1 ignores the requirement 0 ≤ r < m.

questions.q: In the proof that a | b and b | c imply a | c, we write b = a·k and c = b·l. Which integer m shows c = a·m?
questions.explain: c = b·l = (a·k)·l = a·(k·l), and k·l is an integer, so a | c. k + l comes from adding where the proof substitutes and multiplies. b·l equals c, not the multiplier of a. l/k need not be an integer.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
questions.explain: 18 = 4m would need m = 4.5, which is not an integer, so 4 | 18 is false. −3 | 12 since 12 = (−3)(−4); negative divisors are fine. 5 | 0 since 0 = 5·0. 1 divides every integer.

questions.q: What are 2024 div 7 and 2024 mod 7?
questions.explain: 7·289 = 2023, so 2024 = 7·289 + 1. q = 288, r = 8 fails 0 ≤ r < 7, and q = 290, r = −6 uses a negative remainder. Each satisfies a = dq + r but not the remainder condition, so each is tempting.

questions.q: Which integer n satisfies n div 5 = 3 and n mod 5 = 4?
questions.explain: n = d·q + r = 5·3 + 4 = 19. 17 = 3·5 + 2 and 23 = 4·5 + 3 have different remainders. 12 = 3·4 multiplies quotient and remainder, which mixes up their roles.

questions.q: Which congruence is true?
questions.explain: a ≡ b (mod m) means m | (a − b). 38 − 3 = 35 = 7·5, so it is true. 24 − 14 = 10 is not divisible by 6 (lecture example). 15 − 4 = 11 is not divisible by 5, and 20 − 5 = 15 is not divisible by 4.

questions.q: Which integer is congruent to −12 modulo 7?
questions.explain: Add multiples of 7: −12 → −5 → 2 → 9, so −12 ≡ 2 ≡ 9 (mod 7). Check: 9 − (−12) = 21 = 7·3. 12 drops the sign (12 ≡ 5, not 2). 5 and 4 are different residues mod 7 from 2.

questions.q: Find x with 0 ≤ x < 4 such that x ≡ 401³⁷ + 2019 (mod 4).
questions.explain: Reduce term by term. 401 = 4·100 + 1, so 401 ≡ 1 and 401³⁷ ≡ 1³⁷ = 1. 2019 = 4·504 + 3, so 2019 ≡ 3. Then x ≡ 1 + 3 = 4 ≡ 0. Answering 4 forgets the final reduction, since x must satisfy 0 ≤ x < 4.

questions.q: In ℤ₉, compute 7 ·₉ 5.
questions.explain: a ·ₘ b = (a·b) mod m: 35 mod 9 = 35 − 27 = 8. 35 forgets to reduce mod 9. 3 is 7 +₉ 5 = 12 mod 9, which adds instead of multiplying.

questions.q: In ℤ₁₂, compute 9 +₁₂ 8.
questions.explain: (9 + 8) mod 12 = 17 mod 12 = 5. On a 12-hour clock, 8 hours after 9 o'clock is 5 o'clock. 17 is outside ℤ₁₂ = {0, …, 11}.

questions.q: Which list contains ONLY integers congruent to 3 modulo 8?
questions.explain: a ≡ 3 (mod 8) means a = 3 + 8k: …, −13, −5, 3, 11, 19, …. −3 is tempting (it 'looks like' 3), but −3 − 3 = −6 is not divisible by 8. The list 3, 8, 13, 18 steps by 5, and −11 ≡ 5 (mod 8).

questions.q: Suppose a ≡ 4 (mod 7) and b ≡ 5 (mod 7). What is (2a + 3b) mod 7?
questions.explain: Congruences respect + and ·, so 2a + 3b ≡ 2·4 + 3·5 = 23 ≡ 2 (mod 7). 23 forgets to reduce. You never need the actual values of a and b.

questions.q: By definition, a ≡ b (mod m) means:
questions.explain: a ≡ b (mod m) iff m | (a − b), which is equivalent to a mod m = b mod m. 'a mod m = b' is only correct when 0 ≤ b < m (for example 17 ≡ 29 (mod 6) holds, but 17 mod 6 ≠ 29). 'a − b divides m' reverses the divisibility.

questions.q: Find x with 0 ≤ x < 11 such that x ≡ 7·19 (mod 11).
questions.explain: Reduce factor by factor: 19 ≡ 8 (mod 11), so 7·19 ≡ 7·8 = 56 = 55 + 1 ≡ 1. (Check: 133 = 121 + 12 = 11·12 + 1.) 56 is not reduced, and 12 is 133 div 11, the quotient instead of the remainder.

questions.q: What is 10¹⁰⁰ mod 9?
questions.explain: 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9), so 10¹⁰⁰ ≡ 1¹⁰⁰ = 1. This is the same trick as 361 ≡ 1 (mod 5) in lecture. 0 is tempting because 10¹⁰⁰ is huge and 'round,' but the base reduces to 1, so the power does too.

questions.q: What is 2¹⁰ mod 7?
questions.explain: 2³ = 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7), so 2¹⁰ = (2³)³·2 ≡ 1·2 = 2. Check: 1024 = 7·146 + 2. Answering 1 drops the leftover factor: 10 = 3·3 + 1, so one extra 2 remains after the (2³)³ part.

questions.q: Which integer is NOT congruent to 2 modulo 6?
questions.explain: Compute the difference from 2: 16 − 2 = 14, which is not divisible by 6, so 16 ≢ 2 (16 mod 6 = 4). −4 − 2 = −6, 20 − 2 = 18, and 32 − 2 = 30 are all multiples of 6. −4 is often wrongly rejected because it is negative.

questions.q: What is −17 mod 5?
questions.explain: −17 = 5·(−4) + 3 with 0 ≤ 3 < 5, so −17 mod 5 = 3. −17 = 5(−3) − 2 gives −2, but remainders cannot be negative. Answering 2 takes 17 mod 5 and ignores the sign.

questions.q: Today is Tuesday. What day of the week will it be 100 days from today?
questions.explain: Days repeat with period 7, so only 100 mod 7 matters: 100 = 7·14 + 2. Two days after Tuesday is Thursday. Friday comes from using 100 mod 7 = 3, a miscalculation.
